with memory kernels is the standard language of model

locality does not arise. In our setting, the local object
is Markovian and finite-dimensional. Its correspondence
with the nonlocal path measure is not an identity, but
rather a controlled short-memory limit. The novel as-
pect here is the connection: the predictive path measure
of an attention-driven world model is identified as a non-
local Onsager–Machlup measure, that measure is shown

theory from the companion paper [1] is recovered as its
short-memory limit. This is also what distinguishes the
construction from existing generalized Onsager–Machlup
and colored-noise formulations [16, 18], which take the
memory kernel as given. Here, the kernel is generated

Attention enables a world model to condition on its entire history, providing long-term memory
that facilitates long-range predictions. While the local Onsager–Machlup theory in our companion
paper assumes a temporally local predictive action, we investigate the conditions under which this lo-
cality holds. We derive the predictive path measure for latent dynamics that become non-Markovian
due to attention-induced memory, demonstrating that this measure is the projection of a hidden
linear Markov augmentation. Eliminating the auxiliary field results in a nonlocal Onsager–Machlup
action, where memory manifests as a nonlocal quadratic form rather than a force. These kernels
are completely monotone and exactly match a hidden Markov embedding with a finite relaxation
spectrum; otherwise, the dynamics remain fundamentally nonlocal. By expanding the action in
terms of the scale-separation parameter ϵ = τmem/τdyn, we show that the leading order recovers the
local action of the companion paper, establishing locality as the short-memory limit of a nonlocal
theory. We verify the reversible sector of this expansion term by term against an exactly solvable
vector linear model.

General State Space Models.
We note that the term state space model has a very broad meaning which simply represents
the notion of any recurrent process with a latent state. It has been used to refer to many disparate concepts in different
disciplines, including Markov decision processes (MDP) (reinforcement learning (Hafner et al. 2020)), dynamic causal
modeling (DCM) (computational neuroscience (Friston, Harrison, and Penny 2003)), Kalman filters (controls (Kalman 1960)),
hidden Markov models (HMM) and linear dynamical systems (LDS) (machine learning), and recurrent (and sometimes
convolutional) models at large (deep learning).

Foundation models, now powering most of the exciting applications in deep learning, are almost universally based on the
Transformer architecture and its core attention module. Many subquadratic-time architectures such as linear attention,
gated convolution and recurrent models, and structured state space models (SSMs) have been developed to address
Transformers’ computational inefficiency on long sequences, but they have not performed as well as attention on important
modalities such as language. We identify that a key weakness of such models is their inability to perform content-based
reasoning, and make several improvements. First, simply letting the SSM parameters be functions of the input addresses
their weakness with discrete modalities, allowing the model to selectively propagate or forget information along the
sequence length dimension depending on the current token. Second, even though this change prevents the use of efficient

I have enough to give a complete, grounded answer. Here's what the corpus contains on "Markov chain model."

## Markov chain model — findings across the corpus

"Markov chain" shows up in ~20 of the 100 papers, but in three distinct roles. I've separated papers that genuinely *model a system as a Markov chain* from those that only use Markov chain **Monte Carlo** (MCMC) as an inference tool, and from bibliography-only mentions.

### 1. Papers that model a process as a Markov chain (the substantive answer)

**Population genetics — allele frequencies as a Markov chain** (`1606.06090.pdf`)
This is the clearest "Markov chain model" in the corpus. The number of alleles of type B (N_B) in a finite population "is described as a **Markov chain with two absorbing states in 0 and N**, corresponding to the fixation of allele A and B" — the Wright-Fisher model, contrasted with the overlapping-generation Moran model (p. 8). The transition probabilities of this chain are used to derive conditional and unconditioned likelihoods for the selection coefficient; the analysis relies explicitly on "the Markov property of the chains" (p. 5).

**Attention-driven world models — hidden linear-Markov augmentation** (`2607.02154.pdf`, "Path-Measure Dynamics of Attention-Driven World Models")
Attention makes latent dynamics *non-Markovian* (conditioning on full history). The paper's construction restores Markovianity: it builds "a Markovian one for the observed z ∈ ℝᵈ coupled to a hidden auxiliary field w" (p. 3), i.e. a **hidden linear Markov augmentation**. Eliminating the auxiliary field projects the augmented Markov system onto z, generating a memory kernel and a nonlocal Onsager–Machlup action (pp. 1, 4). Locality emerges as the short-memory limit of this Markov embedding (abstract, p. 1).

**High-frequency market making — Markov decision process** (`2607.08291.pdf`, "Robustness in Sequential Decision Making…")
Market making is "formulate[d] … as a finite-horizon **Markov decision process**," then made distributionally robust via Sinkhorn ambiguity sets (p. 5). Its bibliography anchors this in the robust-MDP literature (Nilim & El Ghaoui, Wiesemann et al., Xu & Mannor; pp. 32–34), including "data uncertainty in Markov chains."

**Sequence-model taxonomy — Markov models as state-space models** (`2312.00752.pdf`, Mamba)
Mamba frames "state space model" broadly as "any recurrent process with a latent state," explicitly listing **Markov decision processes (MDP), hidden Markov models (HMM)**, Kalman filters, and linear dynamical systems as instances (p. 4). Mamba itself is a *selective* SSM — a recurrent (Markovian) latent-state model that it argues outperforms Transformers on long sequences (abstract, p. 1).

**Hierarchical topic modeling — Markov process over a tree** (`1301.3570.pdf`)
In the nested Chinese Restaurant Process, "each document selects a path down the tree according to a **Markov process**, which produces a sequence of topics" (p. 1).

### 2. Papers using Markov chain *Monte Carlo* as an inference method (not a Markov-chain model of the domain)

- `0802.0733.pdf` — airplane boarding optimized with an MCMC algorithm (p. 1).
- `2607.06755.pdf` — galaxy gravity/anisotropy fit via the `emcee` affine-invariant MCMC sampler (p. 12).
- `1302.4245.pdf` — Gaussian-process spectral kernels; MCMC proposed for GP hyperparameters (p. 9).
- `1501.05624.pdf` — cites Bayesian probabilistic matrix factorization "using Markov chain Monte Carlo" (p. 10, reference).

### 3. Bibliography-only mention
- `0707.4042.pdf` — cites Keilson, *Markov Chain Models—Rarity and Exponentiality* (p. 15, reference list only).

### Bottom line
There is no single paper in this corpus dedicated to Markov chain modeling. The genuine *models* are domain-specific: an **absorbing Markov chain for allele fixation** in population genetics (`1606.06090`, pp. 5, 8), a **hidden linear-Markov augmentation** of world-model latent dynamics (`2607.02154`, pp. 1–4), a **finite-horizon MDP** for market making (`2607.08291`, p. 5), Markov/HMM/MDP as **state-space-model** instances in Mamba (`2312.00752`, p. 4), and a **Markov process over a topic tree** (`1301.3570`, p. 1). Several other papers use MCMC only as a sampling technique, which is a different thing from modeling a system as a Markov chain.
